title: The Disappearing Bottom Rung in L&D
author: Philippa Hardman
summary: Philippa Hardman analyzed 379 live UK/US job postings for instructional design and L&D roles from mid-2026 and found only four, roughly 1 percent, advertised as junior positions, a dramatic collapse from a field where 53 percent of practitioners had entered within the prior three years as recently as 2023. Drawing on job ads from Multiverse, Motorola Solutions, Amazon, and Coursera, she shows employers now explicitly frame the human's role as judgment and quality control over AI-generated drafts rather than production itself, a pattern corroborated by Stanford data showing under-22-25 employment running 19 percent below expected levels concentrated exactly where AI automates entry-level tasks. Hardman's most consequential argument concerns training: she proposes L&D master's programs keep and expand their theoretical core (needed to write specs and catch subtly wrong AI output) while inverting their studio component from personally crafting assets to writing specs, critiquing AI output, and revising, since the founding assumption that designers build their own media no longer matches the market. Her closing warning is structural rather than sentimental, removing the bottom rung doesn't just close a door for juniors, it eliminates the apprenticeship cycle of doing, feedback, and observing that historically manufactured the field's senior judgment in the first place, and she finds no employer in her sample designing a replacement for it.
points: The data point anchoring the whole piece is stark and falsifiable: out of 379 live job postings, only four (1%) were junior-titled, versus 37% of large-employer hires nationally being entry-level as recently as 2025, and 53% of instructional designers having under three years' experience as recently as 2023.

Hardman's read of the job ads themselves is precise: Multiverse, Motorola, Amazon, and Coursera postings all redefine the human role as 'the judgement layer sitting on top of' AI production rather than the producer, showing the shift is already embedded in hiring language, not just projected.

Her proposed curriculum redesign is concrete and specific: keep the 'science' (theory/evaluation) core since it's what lets a designer 'spot where a fluent AI draft is subtly wrong,' but invert the 'studio' component from asset-crafting to writing specs, critiquing AI output, and revising.

Her closing structural warning reframes junior work as infrastructure, not just labor: 'judgement... was built by doing the work that AI increasingly does for us,' meaning removing the bottom rung doesn't just close a door for juniors, it 'switches off the machine that manufactured the seniors,' and she finds no employer in her sample designing a replacement apprenticeship.
quotes: Out of 379 live postings, only four were advertised as junior roles, that's 1% of all roles. For context, entry-level positions still made up around 37% of hires at large US employers in 2025.
TL;DR: the bottom rung of L&D isn't just narrowing, it's being automated. The humans who remain move up the ladder, and the profession re-forms around a new set of AI and domain specialisms.
The role of the human is not to produce stuff, what juniors used to do, but to be the judgement layer sitting on top of our AI-assisted content pipeline.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, for example, recently reported that employment among 22-25 year olds is running 19% below its expected level, with under-employment concentrated exactly where AI automates tasks.
The studio inverts and reduces because its founding assumption, the designer personally crafts the asset, is now false for most of the market.

Judgement, the skill that the market now pays a premium for, was built by doing the work that AI increasingly does for us. Remove the bottom rung and you don't just close a door for juniors: you also switch off the machine that manufactured the seniors.
